teaser: Circles, triangles and ruled lines, arranged by a painter who said he heard colors.

lesson.text: What does a yellow triangle sound like? If the question seems silly, Wassily Kandinsky would have disagreed. He described colors as having sounds, a crossing of the senses known as synesthesia, and compared yellow to a sharp trumpet blast and deep blue to a cello or an organ. This painting is his attempt to score a whole concert in shapes.

It dates from 1923. Kandinsky was 56 and had just started teaching at the Bauhaus, a German school where art, craft and architecture were taught under one roof. The soft, smoky blots of his earlier work are gone. Everything here could have been drawn with a ruler and a compass.

At the Bauhaus he ran an experiment on his colleagues and students. A questionnaire showed a triangle, a square and a circle, and asked which of three colors belonged in each. His own conviction: the triangle is yellow, the square red, the circle blue.

In the painting, though, he ignores his own table. The circle, his favorite form of these years, turns up in nearly every color, and each time it behaves differently. Four of them sit along the left side.

spots.title: The dark sun
spots.text: A black disc with a violet core, wrapped in a hazy pink glow. It is the largest, heaviest thing on the canvas and pulls at everything else like a planet.

spots.title: Its red moon
spots.text: A flat red circle tucked against the big one, with a faint yellow shimmer around it. Warm, simple, and loud for its size.

spots.title: Yellow in a blue haze
spots.text: A yellow disc with a crisp black outline, floating in a soft blue-green halo. The two colors are opposites, so the yellow seems to push forward.

spots.title: Teal, ringed in pink
spots.text: A dark teal center, a pink ring, a yellow glow. Lines shoot past it on a slant, as if it were a comet crossing the lower edge.

lesson.text: The halos are what make them hum. A hard-edged disc is a sign. A disc with a blurred glow becomes a body giving off light or sound. Kandinsky once said the circle had come to mean to him what the horse had meant in his early pictures: his private emblem.

A concert needs more than long round notes, however. Against the circles he sets everything sharp: angles, spikes, crossing diagonals. Those are the percussion and the strings, and they give the canvas its beat.
Three straight-edged structures that organize the field.

lines.label: The tall peak
lines.text: Two long black lines meet in a needle point near the top edge. This steep angle is the picture's spine and its highest note.

lines.label: The checkered band
lines.text: A sheaf of parallel lines climbs to the upper right corner, with black and patterned squares caught between them like notes on a musical staff.

lines.label: The row of arches
lines.text: One of the few level lines. Half-circles sit on it side by side, each outlined in a different color, a steady pulse beneath the diagonals.

lesson.text: Notice that nothing overlaps in a way that creates depth. No shape hides behind another for long, and the pale ground is neither sky nor wall. It is closer to a blank page of sheet music on which the shapes are written.

Ten years separate this from his previous numbered Composition. In between came war, a return to Russia, and contact there with young artists who built pictures from pure geometry. When he came back to Germany in 1921 he brought that hard clarity with him, and kept his old belief that a painting should act on the soul.

In 1926 he turned his teaching into a book with a title that reads like a recipe for this canvas: Point and Line to Plane. It analyzes what a dot, a line and a flat surface each do to the viewer, one by one.
In Composition VIII, geometry is not cold. Kandinsky treats each shape and color as a voice with its own character, and arranges them the way a composer arranges instruments.

The Nazis closed the Bauhaus in 1933 and Kandinsky left for France. In 1937 dozens of his works, 57 by the usual count, were removed from German museums as “degenerate art,” the regime's insult for modern art it wanted erased.

This canvas was already safe by then. Around 1930 the American collector Solomon R. Guggenheim had bought it, the beginning of a collection of more than 150 Kandinskys. It still hangs in the New York museum that bears his name, a building whose architect also chose one shape above all the others: the circle.

quiz.question: What is synesthesia, as described in the lesson?
options: A crossing of the senses, such as hearing colors
quiz.explanation: Kandinsky described colors as having sounds, a crossing of the senses.

quiz.question: Where was Kandinsky teaching when he painted this?
quiz.explanation: He had recently joined the Bauhaus, a German school of art, craft and architecture.

quiz.question: In his Bauhaus questionnaire, which color did Kandinsky assign to the circle?
quiz.explanation: His rule was yellow triangle, red square, blue circle.

quiz.question: What makes the circles on the left seem to glow?
options: Soft halos of color around them
quiz.explanation: Blurred rings of color around the discs make them look like bodies giving off light.

quiz.question: What is the title of the book Kandinsky published in 1926?
quiz.explanation: Point and Line to Plane grew out of his Bauhaus teaching.

facts.text: Every circle in Composition VIII is blue, following Kandinsky's own rule.
facts.explanation: He ignores his rule here: the circles are black, violet, red, yellow, teal and more.

facts.text: The Nazis removed works by Kandinsky from German museums in 1937.
facts.explanation: They were confiscated as so-called degenerate art.

facts.text: Composition VIII was painted the year after Composition VII.
facts.explanation: Ten years separate the two numbered Compositions.
